claim: Over the last 50 years, anatomical models of memory have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix.
source: Over the last 50 years, anatomical models of memory have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix.
evidence: This claim references established scientific literature and historical models of memory circuits.

claim: Anatomical models of memory downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
source: Such models downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of scientific models based on literature review.

claim: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral testing across three tasks (T-maze alternation, radial-arm maze, geometric discrimination).

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing impairments when intra-maze cues were removed (Stage 2 and 3 of T-maze, rotation in radial-arm maze).

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c- fos ) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data showing reduced c-Fos counts in hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions did not produce widespread reductions in c-fos expression in memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c- fos ) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data showing no significant differences between PCFx and Sham groups.

claim: The findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function dominated by hippocampal inputs.
source: These findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function (those dominated by hippocampal inputs) and herald a new understanding of why specific diencephalic structures are vital for memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that PCFx lesions did not impair memory while VTNx and MTTx lesions did.

claim: The mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: Consequently, the mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei and, from there, to the cingulate (Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969) and prefrontal (Warrington and Weiskrantz, 1982) cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies are unidirectional.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei.
source: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 1985)
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function provide no real function for the mammillary bodies.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing models based on literature review.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function ignore other mammillary body afferents.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing models based on literature review.

claim: The postcommissural fornix lesion disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact.
source: In one group the descending postcommissural fornix (PCF) was lesioned, a procedure that disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact, including those with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous anatomical work and confirmed by mammillary body shrinkage measurements in the current study.

claim: The medial mammillary nucleus is particularly important for memory.
source: Previous clinical and behavioral evidence highlights the particular importance of the medial mammillary nucleus for memory (Vann, 2005, 2010, 2011; Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T-maze alternation and radial-arm maze working memory tasks are sensitive to hippocampal damage.
source: Rats were tested on three behavioral tasks, the first two of which are sensitive to hippocampal damage: T-maze alternation, a working memory task in the radial-arm maze, and a geometric discrimination task (Aggleton et al., 2009; Vann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MTT lesions result in widespread neural hypoactivity as measured by expression of the immediate-early gene c-fos.
source: In addition to impairing spatial memory, MTT lesions also result in widespread neural hypoactivity, as measured by expression of the immediate-early gene c-fos (Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by current c-Fos data.

claim: The final study groups comprised seven Gudden's ventral tegmental nuclei lesion animals (VTNx), eight mammillothalamic tract lesion animals (MTTx), seven postcommissural fornix lesions (PCFx) and eight surgical controls (Sham).
source: A stringent lesion criterion was adopted for final inclusion in the study and, as a consequence, the final groups comprised seven Gudden's ventral tegmental nuclei lesion animals (VTNx), eight mammillothalamic tract lesion animals (MTTx), seven postcommissural fornix lesions (PCFx) and eight surgical controls (Sham).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental group composition.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations.
source: The integrity of the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is important, being the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations and a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs (Satoh and Fibiger, 1986; Sikes and Vogt, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs.
source: The integrity of the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is important, being the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations and a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs (Satoh and Fibiger, 1986; Sikes and Vogt, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nuclei and their cholinergic projections were intact in VTNx animals.
source: The observation that the laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, and subsequently their cholinergic projections, were intact was confirmed by assessing the level of acetylcholinesterase staining in the anteroventral thalamic nucleus (Figure 1C,D) and interpeduncular nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by acetylcholinesterase staining data showing no difference between VTNx and Sham groups in anteroventral thalamic nuclei and interpeduncular nucleus.

claim: Fornix section leads to shrinkage of the mammillary bodies due to loss of white matter.
source: It has been repeatedly shown that fornix section leads to shrinkage of the mammillary bodies (due to loss of white matter).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by current mammillary body area measurements and cell packing density data.

claim: The mean mammillary body area for the PCFx group (1.34 mm²) was significantly smaller than the Sham group (1.79 mm²).
source: The mean mammillary body area (±SEM) for the PCFx group was 1.34 mm2 ± 0.031, making them significantly smaller than the Sham group measurements of 1.79 mm2 ± 0.058 (t(13) = 6.44; p<0.001; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of mammillary body cross-sectional area.

claim: The reduced mammillary body volumes of the PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection.
source: Furthermore, the reduced mammillary body volumes of the present PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection (t(14)=1.67; p>0.1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with previous validated lesion data.

claim: The reduced mammillary body volumes of the PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from rats with complete fornix lesions.
source: Furthermore, the reduced mammillary body volumes of the present PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection (t(14)=1.67; p>0.1) or from rats with complete fornix lesions (t < 1) (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with previous lesion data.

claim: Cell packing density in the medial mammillary nucleus was significantly increased in the PCFx group compared to all three other groups.
source: There was an overall group effect (F(3,27) = 9.96, p<0.001) which reflected a significant increase in the cell packing in the PCFx lesion group compared to all three other groups (Sham, p<0.01; MTTx, p<0.005; VTNx, p<0.001)
evidence: This is supported by cell count data per mm².

claim: The reduced mammillary body volume in the PCFx group reflects loss of white matter and not an overall change in neuronal numbers.
source: This is consistent with the reduced mammillary body volume in the PCFx group reflecting loss of white matter and not an overall change in neuronal numbers (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of reduced volume and increased cell packing density.

claim: The lack of difference in cell packing in the MTTx and VTNx groups, combined with reduced cross-sectional area, is consistent with some medial mammillary body cell loss in these groups.
source: In contrast, lack of difference in cell packing in the MTTx and VTNx groups, combined with reduced cross-sectional area, would be consistent with some medial mammillary body cell loss in these groups.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of reduced volume without increased cell packing density.

claim: Rats can use multiple cue-types to perform spatial alternation tasks.
source: Rats can use multiple cue-types to perform spatial alternation tasks
evidence: This is supported by citation and general knowledge of rodent spatial navigation.

claim: In Stage 1 of T-maze alternation, there was an overall effect of lesion on performance.
source: There was an overall effect of lesion (F(3,27) = 4.93, p=0.007; Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The performance of the VTNx group in Stage 1 of T-maze alternation was significantly worse than the Sham group.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed the performance of the VTNx group to be significantly worse than the Sham group (p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In Stage 2 of T-maze alternation, there was a significant overall group effect on performance.
source: There was a significant, overall group effect on Stage 2 (F(3,27) = 7.12, p=0.001; Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In Stage 2 of T-maze alternation, both the MTTx and VTNx groups performed significantly worse than the Sham group.
source: The group effect reflected the lower scores of both the MTTx (p=0.004) and VTNx (p=0.006) groups compared to the Sham rats.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The lack of impairment in the MTTx group in Stage 1 reflected their use of intra-maze cues.
source: These results suggest that the lack of impairment in the MTTx group in Stage 1 reflected their use of intra-maze cues, such as odor trails.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of impairments across stages where intra-maze cues were systematically removed.

claim: Same place trials were more difficult than different place trials in Stage 2 of T-maze alternation.
source: Overall, same place trials were more difficult than different place trials (F(1,27) = 25.4, p<0.001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In Stage 3 of T-maze alternation, there were overall group differences in performance.
source: An overall analysis of Stage 3 revealed group differences (F(3,27) = 6.28, p=0.002)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In Stage 3 of T-maze alternation, the performances of the VTNx and MTTx groups were significantly worse than those of both the Sham group and the PCFx group.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the performances of the VTNx and MTTx groups were significantly worse than those of both the Sham group (VTNx, p=0.025; MTTx, p=0.019) and the PCFx group (VTNx, p=0.029; MTTx, p=0.023).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Rats find it very difficult to use egocentric cues (e.g., body turns) for delayed alternation.
source: While both direction cues and egocentric cues were available during this stage, previous studies have shown that rats find it very difficult to use egocentric cues (e.g., body turns) for delayed alternation (Baird et al., 2004; Futter and Aggleton, 2006; Pothuizen et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: During radial-arm maze acquisition, there was an overall effect of lesion on the number of errors made.
source: There was an overall effect of lesion (F(3,27) = 4.93, p=0.007; Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: During radial-arm maze acquisition, the VTNx and MTTx groups made significantly more errors than the Sham group.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the VTNx (p=0.006) and MTTx (p=0.009) groups made significantly more errors than the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Following maze rotation in the radial-arm maze task, the groups significantly differed in terms of number of errors made.
source: Following this manipulation the groups significantly differed in terms of number of errors made (F(3,27) = 6.35, p=0.002; Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Following maze rotation in the radial-arm maze task, there were significant differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx and VTNx groups in errors and correct entries.
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed this group effect to be due to differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx (errors, p=0.007; entries, p=0.015) and VTNx groups (errors, p=0.023; entries, p=0.022).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Following maze rotation in the radial-arm maze task, there were significant differences between the PCFx and MTTx groups in errors and correct entries.
source: In addition, there were significant differences between the PCFx and MTTx scores using both error and correct entry values (errors, p=0.030; entries, p=0.014)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All animals completed approximately four trials during the 20 min test session in the novel room for the c-Fos experiment.
source: On the final test day, when animals were tested in the novel room, all animals completed approximately four trials (a trial is completed when all eight arms have been visited) during the 20 min test session (trials completed: VTNx= 4.0 ± 0.0; MTTx = 4.0 ± 0.0; PCFx = 3.9 ± 0.1; Sham = 4.0 ± 0.1), with no group difference in trial numbers (F(3,27) = 1.85, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the c-Fos experiment.

claim: There was a significant group effect in c-Fos counts in the retrosplenial cortex.
source: There was a significant group effect
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data (specific statistics provided in context).

claim: c-Fos counts in the retrosplenial cortex were significantly lower in both the MTTx and VTNx groups compared to the Sham group.
source: Figure 5A shows retrosplenial cortex c-Fos data with significant differences marked between VTNx/MTTx and Sham groups
evidence: This is inferred from Figure 5A showing statistical significance markers for these comparisons.

claim: There was a main group effect in hippocampal c-Fos-positive cell counts.
source: There was a main group effect (F(3,26) = 5.52, p=0.05; Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: c-Fos counts in the hippocampus were significantly higher in the Sham group than both the MTTx and VTNx groups.
source: c-Fos counts in the Sham group were significantly higher than both the MTTx group (p=0.029) and VTNx groups (p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The lesion-induced changes in hippocampal c-fos expression appeared to be largely driven by reductions in CA1.
source: These analyses revealed that the lesion-induced changes in hippocampual c-fos expression appeared to be largely driven by reductions in CA1 as this was the only subfield where there was a significant group difference
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing significant group differences only in CA1 subfield.

claim: There was no group effect in c-Fos counts in the infralimbic cortex.
source: There was no group effect when analysing the infralimbic cortex (F(3,26) =1.23, p>0.3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: There was an overall group effect in c-Fos counts in the prelimbic cortex.
source: In contrast, analyses of the prelimbic cortex revealed an overall group effect (F(3,26) = 5.32, p=0.006; Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells were found in the prelimbic cortex in the MTTx and VTNx groups than in the Sham group.
source: as significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells were found in the MTTx ( p=0.041) and VTNx (p=0.017) groups than in the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: There was no group effect for c-Fos counts in the somatosensory cortex, supramammillary nucleus, lateral septum, or medial septum.
source: There was no group effect for somatosensory cortex (F < 1; Figure 5C), supramammillary nucleus, lateral or medial septum (all F < 1; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The mammillary bodies have a very longstanding association with memory.
source: Although the mammillary bodies (MBs) have a very longstanding association with memory (Gudden, 1896)
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical literature.

claim: Remarkably little is known about the specific contributions of the mammillary bodies to memory.
source: Although the mammillary bodies (MBs) have a very longstanding association with memory (Gudden, 1896), remarkably little is known about their specific contributions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The mammillary bodies have heavy, reciprocal connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei.
source: However, the MBs have heavy, reciprocal connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei whose functional significance has been largely overlooked.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical knowledge and citations.

claim: The functional significance of mammillary body connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei has been largely overlooked.
source: However, the MBs have heavy, reciprocal connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei whose functional significance has been largely overlooked.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract lesions cause c-Fos hypoactivity in numerous sites including the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.
source: The second goal arose because mammillothalamic tract lesions cause c-Fos hypoactivity in numerous sites including the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex (Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by current data.

claim: The ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden is reciprocally connected with the medial mammillary nucleus.
source: The present study focused on the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden as it is reciprocally connected with the medial mammillary nucleus
evidence: This is supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dorsal tegmental nucleus connects with the lateral mammillary nucleus.
source: while the dorsal tegmental nucleus connects with the lateral mammillary nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus forms part of the head-direction network.
source: Although the lateral mammillary nucleus forms part of the head-direction network (e.g., Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Hopkins, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is the loss of the medial mammillary system that appears principally responsible for the spatial memory impairments associated with complete lesions of the mammillary bodies.
source: it is the loss of the medial mammillary system that appears principally responsible for the spatial memory impairments associated with complete lesions of this structure (Vann, 2005, 2010, 2011; Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: The medial mammillary nucleus is always atrophied in the amnesic Korsakoff's syndrome.
source: Furthermore, it is the medial mammillary nucleus that is always atrophied in the amnesic Korsakoff's syndrome (Victor et al., 1989; Kopelman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The MTTx and VTNx groups were equivalently impaired on the radial-arm maze task.
source: The MTTx and VTNx groups were also equivalently impaired on the radial-arm maze task.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing similar impairments in both groups.

claim: Both behavioral tasks indicated that the MTTx and VTNx rats were less able to use allocentric cues and more reliant on intra-maze cues.
source: Thus both behavioral tasks indicated that the MTTx and VTNx rats were less able to use allocentric cues and more reliant on intra-maze cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of impairments across different task stages.

claim: The PCFx animals were not impaired relative to the Shams on any of the behavioral tasks.
source: In contrast, the PCFx animals were not impaired relative to the Shams on any of the behavioral tasks.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing no significant differences between PCFx and Sham groups.

claim: The PCFx animals performed significantly better than both the VTNx and MTTx groups on both the radial-arm maze and T-maze tasks.
source: Consequently, the PCFx animals performed significantly better than both the VTNx and MTTx groups on both the radial-arm maze and T-maze tasks
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons of behavioral data.

claim: The present PCFx lesions were indistinguishable from those that had previously been demonstrated to completely disconnect the hippocampal formation-MB projections.
source: The present PCFx lesions were indistinguishable from those that had previously been demonstrated to completely disconnect the hippocampal formation-MB projections (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous validated lesion data.

claim: The pattern of behavioral impairments was paralleled by the c-Fos findings.
source: The pattern of behavioral impairments was paralleled by the c-Fos findings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing behavioral and c-Fos results.

claim: Reduced levels of c-Fos have been found in the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex following anterior thalamic nuclei lesions.
source: Reduced levels of c-Fos have also been found in this same network of brain regions following anterior thalamic nuclei lesions (Jenkins et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The MTT and VTNg lesions do not result in direct de-afferentation of the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, or prelimbic cortex.
source: However, unlike the c-Fos reduction following anterior thalamic lesions, the current changes reflect 'indirect' effects, as the MTT and VTNg lesions do not result in direct de-afferentation of any of these sites.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of connectivity patterns.

claim: Reduced activity in memory-related networks seems to be a consistent marker of damage to the medial diencephalon in animal models and humans.
source: Although reduced activity in this memory-related network seems to be a consistent marker of damage to the medial diencephalon, in animal models and humans (Joyce et al., 1994; Kapur, 1994; Reed et al., 2003; Savage et al., 2003; Caulo et al., 2005; Anzalone et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It is not known whether reduced activity in memory-related networks contributes to mnemonic deficits or is simply a symptom of the system no longer working effectively.
source: it is not known whether this reduced activity contributes to mnemonic deficits or whether it simply a symptom of the system no longer working effectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Infusions of antisense that block c-Fos activity result in learning and memory deficits.
source: Evidence for the former account comes learning and memory deficits found after infusions of antisense that block c-Fos activity (He et al., 2002; Seoane et al., 2012; Katche et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The present PCFx lesion findings resulted in a 5% reduction in accuracy of T-maze alternation.
source: The present PCFx lesion findings were remarkably similar to those found previously (Vann et al., 2011), for example, they resulted in a 5% reduction in accuracy of T-maze alternation.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and comparison with previous work.

claim: It is possible that the tasks used in the present study did not sufficiently tax the postcommissural fornix pathway.
source: It is possible that the tasks used in the present study did not sufficiently tax this pathway and that greater task demands could result in lesion-induced impairments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the study.

claim: The hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamic nuclei arise from different cell populations.
source: The hippocampal projections to the MBs and anterior thalamic nuclei arise from different cell populations (Wright et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical study.

claim: It is not clear whether the same information is being conveyed by hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: so it is not clear whether the same information is being conveyed (Tsanov et al., 2011) and, therefore, how much replication there is in the system.
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field supported by citation.

claim: There are some situations where anterior thalamic or mammillary body lesion effects can be greater than those of fornix lesions.
source: but there are some situations where anterior thalamic or MB lesion effects can be greater than those of fornix lesions (Tonkiss and Rawlins, 1992; Vann et al., 2000; Jenkins et al., 2004; Aggleton et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The present findings suggest that the more crucial inputs for mammillary body spatial function are from VTNg rather than the hippocampal formation.
source: The present findings clearly suggest that the more crucial inputs for MB spatial function are from VTNg rather than the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of behavioral and c-Fos results showing VTNx impairments but not PCFx impairments.

claim: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta.
source: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta (Kocsis et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological study.

claim: Theta-related cells in the medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function.
source: and theta-related cells in the medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function (Alonso and Llinas, 1992; Kocsis and Vertes, 1994; Bland et al., 1995; Kirk et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: The VTNg have been linked to vigilance states.
source: It is also the case that the VTNg have been linked to vigilance states (Bassant and Poindessous-Jazat, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The VTNg might modulate hippocampal activity.
source: and so might additionally modulate hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the VTNg's role in vigilance and theta activity.

claim: The presumption is that the VTNg lesion effects are primarily via the mammillary bodies.
source: The presumption, based on their dense interconnectivity, is that the VTNg lesion effects are primarily via the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical connectivity.

claim: The VTNg innervates a number of sites including the lateral hypothalamus, preoptic area, medial septum, parts of the reticular pontine nucleus, median raphe nuclei, supramammillary nucleus and ventral tegmental area.
source: The VTNg does, however, innervate a number of other sites, including the lateral hypothalamus, preoptic area, medial septum, parts of the reticular pontine nucleus, median raphe nuclei, supramammillary nucleus and ventral tegmental area (Petrovicky, 1973; Leichnetz et al., 1989; Hayakawa et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: VTNg efferents to sites other than the mammillary bodies appear light.
source: These other VTNg efferents appear light (see Hayakawa and Zyo, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical study.

claim: Lesions of alternative VTNg projection sites rarely result in the pattern of spatial memory impairments seen following VTNg lesions.
source: However, lesions of these alternative sites rarely result in the pattern of spatial memory impairments seen following VTNg lesions (e.g., Sarihi et al., 2000; Pan and McNaughton, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: The lack of Fos changes in the supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides evidence that VTNg effects are not via these routes.
source: In addition, the lack of Fos changes in the supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides some evidence that they are not having their effects via these routes
evidence: This is inferred from the c-Fos data showing no group differences in these regions.

claim: The striking similarity of the VTNg and MTT lesion effects provides support for the VTNg-MB pathway.
source: while the striking similarity of the VTNg and MTT lesion effects in the present study provides further support for the VTNg-MB pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel behavioral and c-Fos results in VTNx and MTTx groups.

claim: In rats, the MTT and VTNg lesion effects appear to be selective for spatial working memory and not due to non-specific effects such as loss of arousal or motivation.
source: In rats, the MTT and VTNg lesion effects appear to be selective for spatial working memory and not due to non-specific effects such as loss of arousal or motivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of impairments (impaired on spatial tasks but not geometric discrimination) and lack of c-Fos changes in control regions.

claim: Both MTTx and VTNx groups were able to acquire a geometric discrimination task at the same rate, and to the same level, as the Sham group.
source: Both MTTx and VTNx groups were able to acquire a geometric discrimination task at the same rate, and to the same level, as the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the water-maze geometric discrimination task.

claim: The geometric discrimination task may be particularly sensitive to lesions within the head-direction system.
source: This task may be particularly sensitive to lesions within the head-direction system (Aggleton et al., 2009; Vann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MTT lesions in the present study are most likely to disconnect the medial mammillary body efferents, while leaving many lateral mammillary body efferents largely intact.
source: As the MTT lesions in the present study are most likely to disconnect the medial MB efferents, while leaving many lateral MB efferents largely intact (Vann and Albasser, 2009)
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and citation to previous work.

claim: The sparing of geometric discrimination performance provides support for the dissociation of two memory systems within the mammillary bodies.
source: this sparing provides further support for the dissociation of two memory systems within the MBs (Allen and Hopkins, 1989; Vann and Aggleton, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective pattern of impairments and supported by citations.

claim: Clinical studies show that both the mammillary bodies and the mammillothalamic tract are important for human memory.
source: Clinical studies show that both the MBs and the MTT are important for human memory, and recollective memory in particular (Dusoir et al., 1990; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Tsivilis et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: For a number of years the very existence of the VTNg in humans had been in doubt.
source: Indeed, for a number of years the very existence of this nucleus in humans had been in doubt (Petrovicky, 1971; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: The structure and connections of the VTNg are remarkably similar across species.
source: However, it is now apparent that the structure and connections of the VTNg are remarkably similar across species (Petrovicky, 1973; Irle and Markowitsch, 1982; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1984; Huang et al., 1992; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: There is only one reported amnesic patient with restricted damage in the VTN area.
source: To date, there is only one reported amnesic patient with restricted damage in the VTN area, but this study is limited in that only CT images were available (Goldberg et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical case study.

claim: The current findings support a novel model of limbic brain interactions.
source: The current findings support a novel model of limbic brain interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the overall pattern of results showing importance of VTNg-MB pathway.

claim: The mammillary bodies have important roles in memory that can be independent of their hippocampal inputs.
source: They show that the MBs have important roles in memory that can be independent of their hippocampal inputs; instead, the results highlight the VTNg.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental results showing VTNx and MTTx impairments but not PCFx impairments.

claim: MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments.
source: Not only do MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments but they also both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing parallel impairments in both groups.

claim: MTT and VTNg lesions both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
source: Not only do MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments but they also both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos data showing reduced activity in hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.

claim: The findings highlight the importance of looking beyond the hippocampus to larger networks of brain regions that contribute to memory.
source: These findings highlight the importance of looking beyond the hippocampus to larger networks of brain regions that contribute to memory (Vann and Albasser, 2011).
evidence: This is a broader implication drawn from the results and supported by citation.

claim: Peak levels of the Fos protein are found approximately 90 min after activation.
source: This time window was chosen as peak levels of the Fos protein are found approximately 90 min after activation (e.g., Sharp et al., 1993; Chaudhuri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on c-Fos expression kinetics.
